rules.violation_condition: A term for a natural phenomenon is formatted in italics.
when: Applies to terms for natural phenomena.
rules.why: This is an independently testable formatting instruction, separate from the surrounding capitalisation rules.

covers.quote: Adjectives and common nouns are in lower case.
Most terms are usually in lower case
This rule applies to many compound nouns.
Specific terms usually take lower case. For example, this rule applies to scientific names for types of clouds.

parts.quote: climate change, global warming, greenhouse gases

rules.quote: Write generic terms for climate and weather in lower case.
rules.violation_condition: A generic climate or weather term, or a specific term normally written in lower case such as a cloud type, has an unwarranted capital letter.
when: Includes compound nouns.
Includes scientific names for types of clouds.
Ordinary sentence-initial capitals are not violations.
Proper nouns and the specifically capitalised names described elsewhere on this page are exceptions.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: generic terms, compound nouns and specific cloud terms are cases of the same lowercase check, not separate findings.

covers.quote: Terms for specific phenomena can take initial capitals
Scientific terms for natural phenomena can include common nouns that combine to form a proper noun.

rules.quote: Use initial capitals when spelling out this kind of scientific term.
rules.violation_condition: A spelled-out scientific term formed from common nouns that together constitute a proper noun lacks the initial capitals of that proper name.
when: Applies when common nouns combine to form the proper name of a natural phenomenon.
Does not apply merely because a scientific term is specific; ordinary terms such as cloud types remain lowercase.
rules.why: G-4: the body supplies the actionable instruction; the heading and preceding sentence establish its scope.

rules.quote: Common shortened forms are in full capitals.
rules.violation_condition: A common shortened form of a proper scientific term for a natural phenomenon is written partly or wholly in lowercase letters.
when: Applies to common shortened forms of the scientific proper names discussed in this section.
rules.why: The casing of a shortened form is a different check from initial capitals in its spelled-out name.

rules.quote: Any non-English names retain the spelling of the original.
rules.violation_condition: A non-English name for a natural phenomenon is written with spelling that differs from its original-language spelling.
when: Applies to non-English names for natural phenomena.
rules.why: Retaining original spelling is an independent requirement, not another case of English capitalisation.

covers.quote: Do this for the given name and for the adjectives and common nouns that appear immediately before the given name. The bureau uses ‘Cyclone’, ‘Tropical Cyclone’ and ‘Severe Tropical Cyclone’ as part of the cyclone’s name.
Use the same rule for hurricanes and typhoons.

rules.quote: Use initial capitals for the names of cyclones.
rules.violation_condition: A cyclone, hurricane or typhoon name has a lowercase initial in its given name or in an adjective or common noun that forms part of the name immediately before the given name.
when: Applies to the given name and the adjectives and common nouns immediately before it that form part of the name.
Includes ‘Cyclone’, ‘Tropical Cyclone’ and ‘Severe Tropical Cyclone’.
The same capitalisation rule applies to hurricanes and typhoons.
rules.why: G-2: the name components and the extension to hurricanes and typhoons are cases of one name-capitalisation check.

parts.quote: Hilda was the first cyclone in the Australian region to make landfall in the 2017–18 season.
Cyclone Hilda made landfall in the 2017–18 season.

rules.quote: Always write ‘Cyclone’ as part of the name unless it is clear from the surrounding text that you are referring to a cyclone.
rules.specification: The page does not define the extent of surrounding text to inspect or a complete test for contextual clarity. An explicit nearby identification as a cyclone is sufficient in its example.
rules.violation_condition: A cyclone is referred to by its given name without ‘Cyclone’, and the surrounding text does not make clear that the reference is to a cyclone.
when: Applies when referring to a named cyclone.
‘Cyclone’ may be omitted when the surrounding text makes the type of event clear.
rules.why: G-2 and G-3: including ‘Cyclone’ is one requirement, with a contextual permission to omit it rather than a second rule.

rules.quote: If the time is a formal period, the name has an initial capital.
rules.violation_condition: The formal-period component of a drought name is written without its initial capital.
when: Applies to drought names based on a formal period.
A date or informal period does not acquire a capital under this rule.
The rule does not capitalise the generic word ‘drought’.
rules.why: G-2: whether the period is formal determines when this single capitalisation check applies.

parts.quote: Ash Wednesday bushfires (Victoria and South Australia, 1983)
Black Friday bushfires (Victoria and New South Wales, 1939)

rules.quote: Bushfires take initial capitals for the adjectival part of their name as well as any proper noun.
rules.violation_condition: The adjectival part or a proper-noun component of a bushfire name lacks its initial capitals.
when: Applies to the adjectival and proper-noun components of bushfire names.
Does not require capitals for generic ‘fire’ or ‘bushfires’.
rules.why: G-2: adjectival and proper-noun components are parts of one bushfire-name capitalisation check.

covers.quote: Floods, earthquakes and tsunamis are named by year, location and event

rules.quote: Use ‘year Location event’ as the naming convention for floods, earthquakes and tsunamis.
rules.violation_condition: A flood, earthquake or tsunami name is expressed in a form other than year followed by location followed by event type.
when: Applies when giving a flood, earthquake or tsunami its event name, rather than making a generic reference to an event.
rules.why: G-2 and G-4: three event types share one naming-structure check; the heading restates it.

rules.quote: Only the location (the proper noun) has an initial capital.
rules.violation_condition: A flood, earthquake or tsunami name has a lowercase location name or an initial capital on the generic event word.
when: Applies to names of floods, earthquakes and tsunamis using the year–location–event convention.
rules.why: Capitalisation and naming order can fail independently, so they are separate checks under the one-finding test.
